Introduction

As a microvascular complication of chronic hyperglycemia in diabetes, diabetic nephropathy (DN) poses
a significant clinical challenge and represents the primary cause of proteinuria in end-stage renal disease
(ESRD) patients. Studies have shown that 15–40% of individuals with diabetes mellitus (DM) may develop
DN during their lifetime [1,2]. With the global prevalence of diabetes expected to reach 643 million by
2030 and 783 million by 2045, the number of DN patients and DN-related ESRD cases is projected to
rise substantially, further increasing mortality and socioeconomic burden. These epidemiological trends
highlight the urgent need to develop new therapeutic strategies [3]. In the last twenty years, DN, a crit­
ical global health problem, has shown substantial increases in both incidence and mortality rates [4]. DN
presents not only serious health challenges for patients but also a considerable socio-economic burden.
Current clinical management primarily targets modifiable risk factors, including hyperglycemia, hyperten­
sion, and proteinuria [5].
   There have been clear advances in clinical management. Although this includes strategies like strict
glycemic control, RAS  inhibitors, SGLT2  inhibitors, and GLP-1 receptor agonists, their primary focus
remains on systemic metabolic risk factors, Their protective effects on renal structure, especially podo­
cytes, remain limited, and many patients continue to progress to ESRD [6]. High cost, adverse effects, and
variable patient response also restrict their widespread application. Therefore, there is an unmet need for
therapeutic agents capable of directly modulating intracellular injury mechanisms in renal cells.
   Excessive ROS production and subsequent oxidative stress, major contributors to DN pathogenesis,
have been shown to be driven by abnormally high glucose and lipid concentrations [7].
   Notably, increased ROS levels induce lipid peroxidation, leading to podocyte damage and the activa­
tion of inflammatory pathways, thereby exacerbating renal injury [8]. Consequently, ROS overproduction
triggers apoptosis, necroptosis, ferroptosis, and autophagy—key forms of programmed cell death  [9].
Autophagy plays an essential role in maintaining podocyte homeostasis, and its suppression under dia­
betic conditions is associated with podocyte loss [10]. In DN models, suppressed autophagic activity is
evidenced by the marked accumulation of the autophagy substrate p62 and reduced expression of
LC3-II. Apoptosis, which plays a central role in DN progression, is induced by various stimuli, including
lipotoxicity, angiotensin, and advanced glycation end products [11]. In podocytes, these stimuli activate
multiple pro-apoptotic signaling pathways. The NRF2/GPX4 signaling pathway, central to cellular antioxi­
dant responses, governs oxidative  stress mitigation and  ferroptosis regulation  [12].  Ferroptosis, an
iron-driven cell death process marked by lipid hydroperoxide buildup, has been identified as a key driver
of DN progression [13]. Autophagy, ferroptosis, and apoptosis, distinct forms of regulated cell death, may
be initiated by shared upstream signals and can either occur concurrently, such as in autophagy-associated
apoptosis, or operate in a mutually exclusive manner.
   Chinese herbal medicine has shown important therapeutic potential in chronic metabolic diseases,
including DN [14]. Hirsutine, a monoterpenoid indole alkaloid isolated from Uncaria rhynchophylla, exhib­
its  multiple pharmacological  activities,  particularly  its  antioxidant and  Anti-cell death  effects  [15].
Accumulating evidence suggests that hirsutine can regulate ROS production, maintain mitochondrial
function, and modulate cell death pathways; however, its role and underlying mechanism in DN remain
largely unexplored [16–18].
   Recent studies have reported renoprotective effects of hirsutine in DN-related contexts, including
modulation of oxidative stress and inflammatory signaling pathways [19,20]. However, whether hirsutine
directly regulates the coordinated interplay among autophagy, apoptosis and ferroptosis in podocytes
under hyperglycemic stress remains unclear. In particular, its potential involvement in the NRF2/GPX4 axis
and autophagy-associated signaling within podocyte-specific injury models has not been systematically
investigated.
   In this study, the conditionally immortalized MPC5 podocyte cell line was selected because MPC5 cells
are widely used to investigate hyperglycemia-induced podocyte injury and closely recapitulate key phys­
iological characteristics, including slit diaphragm structure and cytoskeletal organization. Using this model,
we aimed to evaluate whether hirsutine exerts protective effects against high glucose–induced injury and
whether  its action involves apoptosis suppression, autophagy  regulation, and  ferroptosis  inhibition

                                                                                        Renal Failure      3

through pathways such as PI3K/Akt/mTOR and NRF2/GPX4. This work provides new evidence supporting
the potential renoprotective role of hirsutine and lays a mechanistic foundation for future in vivo validation.


Materials and methods

Reagents and chemicals

The indole alkaloid hirsutine (purity ≥98%, Shanghai Standard Technology Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China; Cat#
ST17300105) was commercially sourced. DMEM (low glucose, Gibco, USA; Cat# 11885-084) and fetal
bovine serum (FBS, Gibco, USA; Cat# 10099-141), along with CCK-8 viability assay kits (Solarbio, Beijing,
China; Cat# CA1210), were used. For oxidative stress quantification, standardized kits manufactured by
Beyotime Biotechnology were employed, including MDA assay kit (Cat# S0131S), GSH assay kit (Cat#
S0053), and SOD activity assay kit (WST-8 method, Cat# S0101S). Antibody panels targeting (i) apoptosis
regulators (e.g., Bax/BCL-2), (ii) autophagy markers (LC3-I/II), and (iii) ferroptosis mediators (GPX4/SLC7A11)
were purchased from Abcam, UK and Proteintech, China (full antibody list with RRID numbers is given
in supplement materials).


Cell cultures and treatment

The  conditionally immortalized MPC5 mouse podocyte  cell  line (Mus musculus, CVCL_A4T8;  iCell
Bioscience Inc., Shanghai, China; Cat# CL-0485) was used. Cells were maintained in low-glucose DMEM
(Gibco, USA; Cat# 11885-084) supplemented with 10% FBS (Gibco, USA; Cat# 10099-141) and 1% penicil­
lin–streptomycin (Solarbio, Beijing, China; Cat# P1400) under standard culture conditions. For prolifera­
tion, cells were incubated at 33 °C in the presence of recombinant interferon-γ. Terminal differentiation
was induced by temperature shift to 37 °C following 10–12 days of culture in interferon-γ-free medium.
Differentiated podocytes (passages 3–5) were exposed to high glucose conditions (30 mM)  in 1%
FBS-containing medium for 24 h, with or without hirsutine treatment. The compound was dissolved in
DMSO (Sigma-Aldrich, USA; Cat# D8418) at a final concentration <0.1% and stored at 4 °C prior to use.


Cell viability assay and morphology examination

The cytoprotective potential of hirsutine was evaluated in MPC5 cells through CCK-8 viability assessment.
Following seeding in 96-well plates, cells were incubated with hirsutine (5–20 μM concentration range)
for 24 h prior to high glucose exposure (24 h). Viability was quantified by measuring 550 nm absorbance
after CCK-8 reagent addition, utilizing a Thermo Scientific Multiskan GO plate reader. Morphological eval­
uation was conducted via Olympus IX71 (Olympus, Japan) inverted microscopy, with documentation of
characteristic cellular changes.


Measurement of ROS levels

ROS detection was performed through three sequential steps: (1) Cellular loading with 10 μM DCFH-DA
(Beyotime, Beijing, China; Cat# S0033S) for 30 min at 37 °C; (2) Enzymatic dissociation into single-cell
suspensions using 0.25% trypsin-EDTA (Solarbio, Beijing, China; Cat# T1300); (3) Quantitative fluorescence
measurement by flow cytometry (FACSCalibur, BD Biosciences, USA). Data analysis was conducted using
FlowJo software (v10.0), with gating strategies established using unstained and hydrogen peroxide-treated
positive controls.


Measurement of GSH, MDA, and SOD levels

We quantified malondialdehyde (MDA), glutathione (GSH), and superoxide dismutase (SOD) concentra­
tions using commercial assay kits according to manufacturers’ protocols((Beyotime, Beijing, China; Cat#

4        B. NI ET AL.

S0131S for MDA, Cat# S0053 for GSH, Cat# S0101S for SOD). Sample processing and reagent application
followed kit-specific guidelines, with final data normalized to total protein content.


ELISA

ELISA kits (Proteintech, Wuhan, China; Cat# KE10007 for IL-6, Cat# KE10008 for IL-10, Cat# KE10002 for
TNF-α) were utilized to quantify inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-10, TNF-α) in MPC5 cell lysates per man­
ufacturer guidelines. Briefly: standards, controls, and samples (100 μL/well) underwent 90-min incubation
at 37 °C. After triple washing, 100 μL of specific antibody was added for 1 h (37 °C). Following another
wash, 100 μL enzyme conjugate was incubated in darkness (30 min, 37 °C). Substrate solution (100 μL) was
then added for 15 min (37 °C) before reaction termination with 100 μL stop solution. Absorbance was
measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader.


JC-1 mitochondrial membrane potential detection kit

JC-1 (Beyotime, Beijing, China; Cat# C2006), a carbocyanine derivative, displays differential fluorescent
behavior based on mitochondrial status. While normal MMP promotes its aggregation into red-emitting
complexes within mitochondria, MMP dissipation causes cytoplasmic dispersion of green-fluorescent
monomers. This  characteristic enables  clear discrimination between apoptotic  cells (predominantly
green) and viable cells (dual red/green fluorescence) through fluorescence microscopy or flow cytometry.


Apoptosis assay

Apoptosis was detected using Annexin V-FITC/PI apoptosis detection kit (Beyotime, Beijing, China; Cat#
C1062S) and analyzed by flow cytometry (FACSCanto  II, BD Biosciences, USA).


Transmission electron microscopy

MPC5 cells were fixed with 2.5% glutaraldehyde (Solarbio, Beijing, China; Cat# P1126) and 1% osmium
tetroxide (Solarbio, Beijing, China; Cat# G1146) After uranyl acetate staining (Solarbio, Beijing, China; Cat#
S2096), samples were epoxy-embedded (EPON resin), polymerized in gelatin capsules (60 °C, 48 h), and
ultrathin-sectioned for TEM (Hitachi, Japan).


Mitochondrial damage scoring

Mitochondrial ultrastructural damage was evaluated using a semi-quantitative scoring system based on
established TEM criteria. Individual mitochondria were manually assessed using the ImageJ “Cell Counter”
plugin and assigned a damage score from 0 to 3 according to cristae integrity and membrane morphol­
ogy(0 = normal, 1 = mild injury, 2 = moderate injury, 3 = severe injury).

Immunofluorescence

MPC5 cells on coverslips were fixed with 4% PFA (Solarbio, Beijing, China; Cat# P1110), permeabilized
with 0.1% Triton X-100 (Solarbio, Beijing, China; Cat# T8200), and blocked. Primary antibodies (4 °C, over­
night) and rhodamine-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG (Abcam, UK; Cat# ab150077) were sequentially
applied. Fluorescence images were acquired using an Olympus inverted microscope.

Western blotting

Cell  lysis was performed on ice (30 min, RIPA + protease  inhibitors). After centrifugation (10,000 ×g,
15 min), supernatants were collected. Protein concentrations were quantified, and samples denatured in
loading buffer (5 min, 100 °C). Equal protein amounts underwent SDS-PAGE separation and PVDF (Millipore,

                                                                                        Renal Failure      5

USA; Cat# IPVH00010) membrane transfer. Membranes were blocked (5% skim milk, RT, 2 h), probed with
primary antibodies (4 °C, overnight), then incubated with HRP-secondary antibodies (RT, 2 h). Band inten­
sities were quantified using ImageJ software and normalized to GAPDH (or β-actin) as the housekeeping
loading control. Protein bands were visualized by ECL and quantified via ImageJ.

Statistical analysis

All experiments were performed at least three times independently. Data are presented as mean ± SD
(n ≥ 3) from three independent biological replicates unless otherwise specified. Statistical analyses used
GraphPad Prism 9.5: one-way ANOVA (Dunnett’s test) or unpaired t-test. Significance thresholds: *p < 0.05,
**p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001, ****p < 0.0001.

Results

Hirsutine alleviated HG-induced cellular damage in MPC5 cells

Consistent with previous reports [21], the optimal concentration for high-glucose (HG) induction in MPC5
cells was identified as 30  mM (Figure 1(a)). Based on this, three concentrations of hirsutine (5, 10, and
20  μM) were selected to evaluate its effects on HG-stimulated MPC5 cells (Figure 1(b)). Cell viability under
hirsutine treatment was quantified via CCK-8 assay. The results demonstrated that 5  μM hirsutine partially
alleviated HG-induced cytotoxicity, while 10 and 20  μM treatments led to a more pronounced restoration
of cell viability after 24 h (Figure 1(c)). Importantly, a 24-h treatment period was selected according to pre­
vious MPC5 studies, which commonly employ 24 h HG exposure and drug intervention to assess cytotoxic­
ity, inflammation, and autophagy responses [22]. The protective effect of hirsutine was further evidenced
by its ability to alleviate HG-induced morphological abnormalities, including cell shrinkage, loss of podocyte
process-like extensions, and cytoplasmic vacuole formation (Figure 1(d)). The inflammatory response to

hyperglycemic conditions was evidenced by elevated cytokine production (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6) in MPC5 cells
(Figure 1(e)). Hirsutine intervention significantly suppressed HG-induced cytokine overexpression (p < 0.05),
suggesting its therapeutic potential may involve inhibition of NF-κB or MAPK inflammatory pathways.

Hirsutine pretreatment attenuated HG-induced oxidative stress in MPC5 cells

To further investigate the effects of hirsutine on HG-induced oxidative stress and cellular damage in
MPC5 cells, we examined oxidative biomarkers, including MDA, GSH, and SOD, to evaluate both oxida­
tive injury and antioxidant capacity. MDA levels were markedly elevated under hyperglycemic condi­
tions, increasing from 5.41 ± 2.81 μmol/L in the control group to 32.62 ± 4.84 μmol/L in the HG group.
Hirsutine treatment significantly reduced MDA levels to 14.91 ± 1.07 μmol/L. Conversely, intracellular
GSH content decreased from 65.27 ± 11.44 μmol/L in the control group to 16.33 ± 5.72 μmol/L in HG
group and was partially restored following hirsutine administration. Similarly, SOD activity declined
markedly under HG stimulation (15.32 ± 4.38 U/mL) and recovered to 55.38 ± 8.06 U/mL after hirsutine
treatment (Figure 2(a)).
  Flow cytometry and fluorescence microscopy detected cellular ROS accumulation. ROS relative fluores­
cence intensity increased to 2.17 ± 0.05 in the HG group and was reduced to 1.31 ± 0.04 following hirsu­
tine  intervention.  This  result  demonstrated  that  hirsutine  markedly  attenuated  HG-induced ROS
accumulation (Figure 2(b,c)). Since oxidative stress indicators such as MDA, GSH, and SOD are closely
linked to programmed cell death pathways, and given that autophagy plays a critical role in ROS clear­
ance, we hypothesized that hirsutine’s cytoprotective effects might involve the modulation of autophagy,
as well as the suppression of ferroptosis and apoptosis.
  To validate this hypothesis, specific pharmacological modulators were employed: ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1)
as a ferroptosis inhibitor, Z-VAD-FMK as a pan-caspase inhibitor for apoptosis, and rapamycin as an auto­
phagy activator. Notably, all three interventions led to improved cell viability under HG stimulation. These

Hirsutine suppressed HG-induced apoptosis in MPC5 cells

Mitochondrial dysfunction is a hallmark of apoptosis, with the loss of MMP serving as a key indicator
of mitochondrial damage [23]. The integrity of MMP in MPC5 cells post-HG exposure was assessed
using the JC-1 staining method. HG treatment led to a marked reduction in MMP, indicative of mito­
chondrial depolarization, when compared to control cells. Notably, hirsutine treatment significantly
attenuated the HG-induced loss of MMP (Figure  3(a)). To further investigate hirsutine’s ability to
inhibit apoptosis, Annexin V/PI dual staining was performed. This analysis revealed a marked eleva­
tion in the proportions of both early and late apoptotic cells following HG stimulation. However,
hirsutine administration effectively mitigated HG-induced apoptosis in a dose- and time-dependent
manner, with the most pronounced effect observed at 20  μM after 24 h (Figure 3(b)). We additionally
analyzed  apoptosis-associated   proteins.  Hirsutine  administration  dose-dependently  reduced
pro-apoptotic BAX and cleaved caspase-3 levels while enhancing anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 expression
(Figure 3(c)).

Hirsutine-regulated autophagy-associated signaling in HG-treated MPC5 cells

Autophagy dysfunction is widely recognized as an indicator of podocyte injury and apoptosis both in
vitro and in vivo [24]. Given the observed protective effect of hirsutine against apoptosis in MPC5 cells,
it remained unclear whether this protection involves the regulation of autophagy-related pathways, par­
ticularly those contributing to apoptosis induced by autophagy downregulation. Further investigation
was therefore warranted. LC3 and p62 are widely used as molecular markers for monitoring autophago­
some formation and autophagic flux [25]. Autophagy inhibition is typically characterized by a reduced
LC3-II/LC3-I  ratio and elevated p62 accumulation, both of which contribute to podocyte apoptosis.
Immunofluorescence staining further confirmed the expression patterns of autophagy markers LC3 and
p62. Compared with the model group, hirsutine treatment significantly downregulated p62 expression
and upregulated LC3-II levels (Figure  4(a)), indicating autophagy-associated alterations in HG-treated
MPC5 cells. In addition, the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway, which is closely associated with impaired

Discussion

Diabetic nephropathy (DN) is primarily characterized by progressive podocyte injury, a pivotal early event
that drives glomerular filtration barrier disruption. Although DN involves complex whole-kidney pathol­
ogy, the present study specifically focuses on podocyte-intrinsic mechanisms responsible for cytotoxicity
under hyperglycemic conditions [4]. A large body of evidence identifies oxidative stress as the central
pathological driver in podocytes, where excessive ROS production promotes inflammation, disturbs redox
homeostasis, and triggers multiple regulated cell death pathways. While both apoptosis and ferroptosis
involve  lipid peroxidation, their upstream regulators and execution mechanisms are distinct [27,28].
Autophagy, a vital cellular mechanism for maintaining homeostasis, alleviates oxidative stress and inflam­
mation, thereby contributing to renal protection [29]. Furthermore, oxidative stress orchestrates crosstalk
between apoptosis and  ferroptosis, two  evolutionarily  distinct regulated  cell death pathways now
acknowledged as central mediators of diabetic renal injury [30]. Apoptosis  is caspase-dependent and
mitochondria-regulated, whereas ferroptosis  is iron-dependent and marked by catastrophic lipid ROS
accumulation. Therefore, distinguishing oxidative stress–induced apoptosis from ferroptosis is essential to
accurately interpret podocyte injury mechanisms.
  Beyond its core bioactivities in inflammation suppression, apoptosis modulation, and oxidative stress
attenuation, hirsutine demonstrates pleiotropic regulatory capacities across diverse pathological cascades
[18]. Hirsutine significantly reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine expression in MPC5 cells. Although cyto­
kine measurements in podocyte lysates primarily reflect cell-intrinsic inflammatory responses, these find­
ings remain biologically meaningful because podocytes are active participants in the local inflammatory

microenvironment during DN progression. It is important to note that, in vivo, macrophages, T cells, and
other immune cells also contribute to the overall cytokine milieu; therefore, our data mainly capture the
podocyte-specific component of this process while broader immune-cell interactions warrant further
investigation.
  Although the precise pathogenic mechanisms underlying DN remain unclear, accumulating evidence
suggests that oxidative stress is a key driver of disease progression. Elevated ROS levels contribute to
renal cell injury, ultimately resulting in renal insufficiency [31]. The antioxidant defense system is incapac­
itated by ROS overproduction, leading to suppressed activity of pivotal redox regulators, specifically SOD
and GSH, along with parallel escalation in malondialdehyde levels, the principal biomarker of lipid per­
oxidation [32]. Previous studies have reported that hirsutine attenuates oxidative stress induced by vari­
ous pathological stimuli  [18]. In this study, hirsutine markedly reduced intracellular ROS levels and
enhanced antioxidant enzyme activities in MPC5 cells. Although the magnitude of ROS reduction did not
completely mirror the degree of SOD and GSH restoration, such non-parallel patterns are commonly
observed in redox biology. They may reflect differences in the temporal dynamics of ROS scavenging
versus enzymatic regulation, as well as the  distinct  sensitivities of biochemical assays to oxidative
changes. These observations highlight the multilayered nature of redox homeostasis in podocytes and
suggest that hirsutine may act at several regulatory nodes along the oxidative stress cascade. Further
kinetic studies would help delineate how these pathways are coordinated under hyperglycemic condi­
tions. As a highly regulated cellular suicide mechanism, apoptosis performs critical physiological func­
tions  including  tissue  homeostasis  maintenance, developmental  patterning  coordination, and  cell
population control [33]. Dysregulated apoptosis serves as a key molecular driver in numerous disease
states, with well-documented involvement in diabetic kidney disease development [34]. Additionally, TEM
revealed ferroptosis-related ultrastructural changes, including mitochondrial condensation and cristae
loss under HG stimulation. These morphological alterations were consistent with biochemical evidence of
enhanced lipid peroxidation. Because TEM and biochemical assays were performed on separate prepara­
tions, the correspondence between  structural and molecular  indicators  reflects  overall rather than
single-sample correlations. Even so, the convergence of both datasets supports ferroptotic involvement
in podocyte injury, and future integrated approaches may help refine these associations. Cellular homeo­
stasis  under  basal  conditions   is  maintained  through  the  precisely  orchestrated  interplay  of
autophagy-mediated cellular renewal and apoptosis-regulated programmed cell death. However, in DN,
reduced protective autophagy alongside increased podocyte apoptosis may contribute significantly to
renal injury [21].
   Furthermore, we examined the role of autophagy in HG-induced injury of MPC5  cells. Autophagy
dysfunction is recognized as a contributing factor to podocyte damage, and previous studies have shown
that HG conditions suppress autophagic activity [35]. LC3 operates as a central regulator in autophago­
some formation, with its proteolytic processing and lipid modification constituting a key regulatory node.
The conversion from soluble LC3-I to phosphatidylethanolamine-anchored LC3-II serves as a definitive
biochemical marker for monitoring autophagy induction [36]. Additionally, autophagy activation induces
the degradation of p62, a substrate of autophagy [37]. Our findings demonstrated that hirsutine treat­
ment induced coordinated changes in autophagy-associated markers, including altered LC3 processing
and reduced p62 levels. However, these observations reflect static autophagy-related alterations rather
than definitive autophagic flux. The study additionally interrogated the PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling path­
way, an evolutionarily conserved metabolic hub that orchestrates critical cellular decisions ranging from
cycle progression and differentiation programming to survival pathway activation [38]. Hirsutine treat­
ment reduced the phosphorylation levels of Akt and mTOR, suggesting that hirsutine may promote auto­
phagy in MPC5 cells by suppressing the PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling pathway.
  Although  p62  reduction  can   indicate  enhanced  autophagic   flux,    it  may   also   reflect
ferritinophagy-mediated degradation of ferritin, which increases the labile iron pool and promotes ferro­
ptosis. However, in our study, hirsutine consistently reduced lipid ROS, preserved GPX4 expression, and
did not increase NCOA4  levels, suggesting that ferritinophagy was not activated. Instead, hirsutine
appears to promote general, cytoprotective autophagy that decreases ROS burden and mitigates ferro­
ptosis. This dual relationship between autophagy and ferroptosis highlights the importance of pathway
context [39].

  The transcription factor Nrf2 serves as a principal orchestrator of cytoprotective responses, governing
both oxidative stress adaptation pathways and regulatory networks that determine cellular vulnerability
to ferroptosis [40]. Transcriptional upregulation of Nrf2 establishes a robust defense mechanism against
ferroptotic cell death. Current research consensus confirms that Nrf2-mediated GPX4 signaling activation
promotes the biosynthesis of radical-scavenging enzymes, creating a dual protective  effect against
ROS-mediated damage and iron-catalyzed lipid peroxidation [41]. In the present study, Experimentally,
HG suppressed core ferroptosis suppressors (GPX4/SLC7A11/Nrf2/HO-1/NQO1) while upregulating ACSL4,
a key regulator of lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis. Hirsutine treatment rectified these pathogenic alter­
ations and protected against HG-induced nephrotoxic effects. However, in the absence of functional val­
idation experiments (such as NRF2 knockdown or pharmacological modulation), these findings should be
interpreted as correlative evidence rather than definitive proof of NRF2-dependent ferroptosis inhibition.
Future studies incorporating loss-of-function approaches will be required to determine whether NRF2
activation is necessary for the protective effects of hirsutine.
  Although previous reports have demonstrated beneficial effects of hirsutine in DN models, our study
extends these findings by systematically evaluating apoptosis, autophagy-associated signaling alterations,
and ferroptosis-related molecular signatures within the same podocyte-specific hyperglycemic model.
Unlike earlier studies that primarily focused on inflammatory or oxidative pathways, the present work
integrates multiple regulated cell death-associated mechanisms and highlights a potential link between
NRF2/GPX4-related antioxidant responses and ferroptosis-associated biochemical changes [42].
   Unlike previous studies primarily focusing on anti-inflammatory or antioxidant properties of hirsutine
in renal models, our study systematically evaluated apoptosis, autophagy-associated  signaling, and
ferroptosis-related biochemical signatures within the same podocyte model, highlighting a coordinated
regulatory pattern.
  We did not compare hirsutine with SGLT2 or GLP-1 drugs because these agents primarily exert sys­
temic glucose-lowering effects, whereas the present study was specifically designed to investigate direct
podocyte-specific cellular mechanisms; such comparisons will require in vivo DN models. Limitations of
the current study also include the absence of direct autophagic flux assays and the lack of functional
NRF2 validation. While LC3/p62 expression, TEM morphology, and pharmacological modulators provide
convergent mechanistic evidence, we acknowledge these gaps. Planned follow-up work will incorporate
autophagic flux evaluation, ARE-luciferase and NRF2 genetic manipulation, and in vivo studies assessing
renal function and albuminuria to further strengthen the mechanistic and translational significance of
hirsutine.

Conclusions

Collectively, our findings indicate that hirsutine alleviates HG-induced podocyte injury, as reflected by
quantifiable improvements in cell viability, reductions in ROS and apoptotic markers, and modulation of
ferroptosis-related lipid peroxidation alongside enhanced autophagy-associated protein changes. However,
these observations are limited to an in-vitro MPC5 model and reflect pathway-associated alterations
rather than definitive mechanistic causation. Therefore, in vivo studies assessing renal function, inflamma­
tory responses, and systemic metabolic regulation are required to validate these podocyte-specific effects
within the broader context of diabetic nephropathy.
   Future directions of the study should prioritize translating the present in-vitro findings into physiolog­
ically relevant models by validating the renoprotective effects of hirsutine in well-established in vivo
diabetic nephropathy models, with comprehensive assessment of renal function, albuminuria, histopatho­
logical changes, and podocyte integrity. Mechanistically, future work should incorporate dynamic auto­
phagic flux assays (e.g. tandem fluorescent LC3 reporters) and genetic or pharmacological manipulation
of NRF2 to definitively establish causal links between autophagy activation, NRF2/GPX4 signaling, and
ferroptosis suppression. Given the complex  crosstalk among apoptosis, autophagy, and  ferroptosis,
systems-level approaches such as transcriptomics and metabolomics may further elucidate upstream reg­
ulatory networks modulated by hirsutine under hyperglycemic stress. In addition, comparative studies
with current standard-of-care agents, including SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists, are war­
ranted in animal models to determine potential additive or synergistic effects. Finally, pharmacokinetic,

message.content: This study investigated the protective effects of hirsutine, an indole alkaloid, against high glucose (HG)-induced injury in MPC5 podocytes, an in vitro model of podocyte dysfunction in diabetic nephropathy (DN). MPC5 cells were exposed to 30 mM HG with or without hirsutine (5–20 μM), and cell viability, oxidative stress, apoptosis, and ferroptosis were assessed. Hirsutine significantly improved cell viability, reduced intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, and suppressed apoptosis, indicating its cytoprotective role. It also modulated autophagy by altering LC3 and p62 expression and inhibited ferroptosis by upregulating NRF2 pathway markers and reducing lipid peroxidation. These findings suggest that hirsutine exerts protective effects through the coordinated regulation of apoptosis, autophagy, and ferroptosis. However, the study is limited to an in vitro model and lacks direct autophagic flux assessment and genetic validation of NRF2 dependency. The results highlight hirsutine's potential as a therapeutic candidate for DN, but further in vivo studies are needed to confirm its efficacy and mechanism of action.

Introduction

The COVID-19 pandemic caused an increase in the global age-standardized all-cause mortality rates. In
2020–2021, an estimated 16 million excess deaths occurred, either directly due to the severe acute
respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection, or indirectly due to social or behavioral
changes during the pandemic, such as delaying healthcare visits.1 Large-scale vaccination was the most
effective strategy to prevent illness, hospitalization and mortality due to COVID-19,2 and effective vaccines
were developed with unprecedented speed. Scientific advances, such as the prior research on mRNA and
adenoviral vector platforms, provided the means to enable accelerated vaccine development.3
  Although COVID-19 has transitioned from a pandemic to an endemic disease,4,5 SARS-CoV-2 remains
a leading cause of severe viral respiratory illness, particularly among older adults,6–8 and wastewater
surveillance  shows  elevated  levels  of SARS-CoV-2  post-Omicron,  suggesting  continued  virus
circulation.9–11 To prevent adverse outcomes, vaccination remains the best strategy, and the World
Health Organization currently recommends that all adults and children who were not yet vaccinated receive
one dose of a COVID-19 vaccine, or two to three doses for immunocompromised individuals.12 Adults over
50 or 60 y old (depending on the country) and adults with comorbidities should be revaccinated 12 months
after the most recent dose.12 Adults over 75 or 80 y old and adults over 50 or 60 y old with comorbidities
should be revaccinated 6–12 months after the most recent dose.12
  As SARS-CoV-2 evolution reduces vaccine effectiveness, new vaccines and periodic vaccine composition
updates are required.13,14 In addition, there is a need for vaccines with lower antigen doses and better
thermostability.15
   Previously, we conducted an open-label phase 1 clinical study in healthy adults to assess the safety and
immunogenicity of an mRNA COVID-19 vaccine encoding the SARS-CoV-2 Omicron BA.1 spike protein
(CV0501 mRNA vaccine).16 In this phase 2, observer-blind, randomized, active-controlled study with
a licensed, bivalent mRNA COVID-19 comparator containing the then-recommended viral components
for 2022–2023,17 we investigated the reactogenicity, safety and immunogenicity of two investigational
mRNA COVID-19 vaccines (one monovalent and one bivalent).



Patients and methods

Study design

This was a randomized, multi-center, active-controlled, observer-blind phase 2 study (ClinicalTrials.gov:
NCT05960097). Participants were randomized (1:1:1:1:1) to receive either one of three dose levels of
a bivalent mRNA COVID-19 vaccine encoding ancestral D614G and Omicron BA.4–5 spike proteins
(CV0701 mRNA vaccine; CV0701-Low group: 3 + 3 µg of mRNA encoding for each antigen, CV0701-
Med group: 6 + 6 µg of mRNA encoding for each antigen, CV0701-High group: 12 + 12 µg of mRNA
encoding for each antigen), a monovalent mRNA COVID-19 vaccine encoding the Omicron BA.4–5
spike protein (CV0601 mRNA vaccine; CV0601 group: 12 µg of mRNA encoding for the antigen) or
a licensed comparator vaccine (Pfizer-BioNTech’s bivalent Original Wuhan/Omicron BA.4–5 mRNA
vaccine; comparator group: 15 + 15 µg of mRNA encoding for each antigen). A central randomization
system was used, and study intervention was assigned by means of permuted block randomization using
country, previous known SARS-CoV-2 infection (yes, no) and age (<65 y, ≥65 y) as stratification factors.
  The participants, site and sponsor personnel involved in the clinical evaluation of the participants were
blinded to treatment allocation. Other study personnel, such as the study pharmacist, could be aware of the

                                                     HUMAN VACCINES & IMMUNOTHERAPEUTICS       3


treatment assignment. The vaccines were prepared and administered by unblinded qualified study person­
nel who were not involved in data collection, evaluation, review or entry of any study endpoint.
  The present study focused on the ancestral D614G and Omicron BA.4–5 variants.


Study population

Participants ≥18 y of age who were generally healthy or had a stable medical condition and had provided
written informed consent were eligible for enrollment. Additionally, participants were required to have
completed at least a primary vaccination series, with or without a booster, with an approved or authorized
mRNA COVID-19 vaccine at least three months prior to randomization. Vaccination history with mRNA
COVID-19 vaccines was based on locally accepted documentation of vaccination.
  The main exclusion criteria were a history of a SARS-CoV-2 infection within three months prior to study
intervention administration, or a history of an immunosuppressive or immunodeficient condition resulting
from disease, or the use of immunosuppressants or immune-modifying drugs for 14 consecutive days or
more within three months prior to study intervention administration. Participants with a history of
myocarditis, pericarditis, idiopathic cardiomyopathy, or with any medical condition that increases the
risk of myocarditis or pericarditis were also excluded. Full inclusion and exclusion criteria are listed in the
Supplementary materials.


Ethics

The study protocol, informed consent forms and other relevant study-related documents were reviewed and
approved by the Bellberry Human Research Ethics Committee (2023–05-556) before study initiation. The
study was conducted in accordance with the protocol and consensus ethical principles derived from
international guidelines, including the Declaration of Helsinki, Council for International Organizations
of Medical Sciences International Ethical Guidelines, applicable International Council for Harmonization
Good Clinical Practice guidelines, as well as other applicable laws and regulations.


Objectives

The primary objectives of the study were to evaluate: (1) the reactogenicity and safety of the CV0701 and
CV0601 mRNA vaccines, and (2) the immunogenicity in terms of serum neutralizing titers at Day 29 of the
CV0701 and CV0601 mRNA vaccines, compared to a licensed mRNA COVID-19 vaccine. Secondary
objectives were to further characterize the humoral immune response in terms of serum neutralizing titers,
fold increase from baseline of serum neutralizing titers and seroresponse rates. As tertiary objectives, the
humoral immune response in terms of binding of immunoglobulin (Ig)G anti-spike protein and the cell-
mediated immunity (CMI) were characterized. The full description of each study endpoint is listed in the
Supplementary materials.


Procedures

After informed consent was obtained, baseline demographic data, such as age, sex, race and ethnicity, as well
as vital signs were recorded. A complete physical examination was performed and recorded. Medical and
vaccination history was obtained by interviewing the participant and by reviewing the participant’s medical
records.
   Enrolled females of childbearing potential received the study intervention only after a negative urine
pregnancy test. All vaccines were administered on Day 1 as a single, intramuscular dose in the deltoid,
preferably in the non-dominant arm (Figure 1).
   Solicited administration-site events (injection-site pain, redness, swelling and lymphadenopathy) or
solicited systemic events (fever, fatigue, headache, chills, myalgia and arthralgia) that occurred during the
7d follow-up period after vaccination (Day 1–Day 7) were recorded by the participant using an electronic
diary (eDiary). All other adverse events (AEs) that occurred within the same timeframe were recorded by
the investigator. On Day 8 (±1 d), a telephone contact took place between the site staff and the participant,

   All unsolicited AEs were monitored for a 28-d follow-up period (Day 1–Day 28) (Figure 1). Participants

the AE and documented the event in the participant’s records during this contact, or by reviewing the

(Day 1–Day 181) (Figure 1).
   Additional visits were planned for all participants on Day 29 (±3 d), Day 91 (±7 d) and Day 181 (±7 d)
after vaccine administration to collect blood samples (Figure 1). Immunogenicity was assessed by measur­
ing serum neutralizing titers against a pseudovirus bearing the Omicron BA.4–5 or the ancestral D614G
spike protein, as previously described.16,18 To characterize the CMI response, the frequency of SARS-CoV-2
spike-specific polypositive CD4+/CD8+ T cells expressing at least two different markers with at least one
cytokine, among CD40 ligand, 41-BB, interleukin (IL)-2, tumor necrosis factor-α; interferon (IFN)-γ, IL-13
and IL-17 upon in vitro stimulation, was assessed by an intracellular cytokine staining assay, as published
previously,16 and summarized descriptively by vaccine group at Day 1 and Day 8. CMI was also assessed
using a T-cell phenotyping panel (Supplementary materials) which measures the frequency of in vivo
activated (human leukocyte antigen [HLA]-DR+ and CD38+) CD8+ T cells.


Statistical methods

Approximately 415 participants were planned to be enrolled and randomized in the study. The current
study did not include formal hypothesis testing. Statistical methods aimed at estimation with 95% con­
fidence intervals (CIs), without multiplicity adjustments.
   Safety endpoints were analyzed descriptively. The occurrence of solicited events, unsolicited AEs,
MAAEs, SAEs and AESIs was analyzed as the percentage of participants reporting an event. The analysis
of unsolicited AEs, MAAEs, SAEs and AESIs was based on the exposed set, i.e., all participants who received
study intervention administration. The analysis of solicited events was based on the eDiary set,  i.e.,
participants from the exposed set who had eDiary data available.

                                                     HUMAN VACCINES & IMMUNOTHERAPEUTICS       5


   All immunogenicity analyses were based on the per-protocol set,  i.e., all exposed participants who
complied with the protocol, had pre-dose and Day 29 results available, and did not experience any events
that may have interfered with immunogenicity. For humoral immunogenicity analyses, adjusted geometric
mean titers (GMTs) were obtained from an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) model on log10-transformed
anti-neutralizing titers and then back-transformed to the original scale. The model included the vaccine
group, previous known SARS-CoV-2 infection (yes, defined by self-reporting or positive nucleocapsid [N]
protein at pre-vaccination, no), age (<65 y, ≥65 y) and log10-transformed pre-vaccination titer as fixed
effects. Seroresponse was defined as an ≥4-fold increase in neutralizing titer from pre- to post-vaccination, if
the pre-vaccination titer was above the lower limit of quantification (LLoQ), or a post-vaccination titer ≥4
times the LLoQ when pre-vaccination titers were below the LLoQ.
   All analyses were conducted using SAS version 9.4.


Results

Study participants

Between August 01, 2023 and April 17, 2024, 491 participants were screened and 427 participants were
enrolled in 13 Australian study centers. Of these, 425 participants were vaccinated, and 381 were included in
the per-protocol set at Day 29 (Figure 2). Twelve out of 425 participants discontinued the study early; none
of these discontinuations were due to an AE.



Demographics

Overall, the mean age (±standard deviation) at study intervention administration was 53.6 ± 16.4 y, with
most participants (69.4%) in the 18–64 y of age category. The median (quartile [Q]1–Q3) body mass index
ranged from 27.5 (23.8–31.5) in the CV0701-Med group to 28.7 (24.6–31.7) in the CV0601 group (Table 1).
Overall, 48.5% of participants were female, 87.5% were White, and 96.9% were not of Hispanic or Latino
ethnicity. Prior SARS-CoV-2 infection was reported for 80.9% of participants; 74.4% of the participants
were positive prior to vaccination using a serology test based on a binding antibody specific to SARS-CoV-2
N protein. A median number of four prior COVID-19 vaccinations, which occurred > 6 months prior to
study intervention administration for most (70.6%) participants, was reported. Vital signs were comparable

Safety

Overall, compliance with eDiary completion was ≥99.5% across all groups. Within seven days post-
vaccination, injection-site pain was the most frequently reported solicited administration-site event in
all groups, ranging from 39.1% (34/87) in the CV0701-Low group to 63.5% (54/85) in the comparator

Immunogenicity

At Day 29 post-vaccination, geometric means of serum neutralizing titers against a pseudovirus encoding
the Omicron BA.4–5 spike protein increased with increasing dose in the groups receiving CV0701 (Figure 4
(A)). The CV0601 group had a numerically higher GMT compared to the CV0701-High group, and all
groups but the CV0701-Low dose group had numerically higher GMTs compared to the comparator group,
with overlapping CIs (Figure 4(A)). A decrease in neutralizing titers was observed at three months (Day 91),
and further at six months (Day 181) post-vaccination, compared to Day 29; however, the GMTs remained
above baseline for all groups up to Day 181 (Figure 4(A)). The adjusted GMT ratio (investigational vaccine
over comparator) at Day 29 ranged from 0.73 (95% CI: 0.55–0.99) to 1.23 (0.91–1.66) for the CV0701
groups and was 1.29 (0.95–1.74) for the CV0601 group (Supplementary Table S2).
  A similar pattern was observed for the geometric means of serum neutralizing  titers against
a pseudovirus encoding the ancestral D614G spike protein at all timepoints, with a dose-dependent rise
in the GMTs at Day 29 in the CV0701 groups, and a tendency for a higher GMT in the CV0601 group,
which declined but persisted up to Day 181 (Figure 4(B)). At Day 29, adjusted GMT ratios (investigational
vaccine over comparator) ranged from 0.77 (95% CI: 0.61–0.97) to 1.08 (0.85–1.38) for the CV0701 groups
and was 1.08 (0.85–1.38) in the CV0601 group. In all but the CV0701-Low group, the adjusted GMT ratios
were around or above 1.00 up to Day 181 (Supplementary Table S2).
  For the Omicron BA.4–5 variant, seroresponse rates were approximately 50% for all groups, except for
the CV0701-Low group. They were comparable to the comparator vaccine for the Omicron BA.4–5 antigen,
but lower for the ancestral D614G antigen (17.9% to 29.3%, comparator 35.0%), although the 95% CIs
overlapped (Table 3).
   Similar results as for the geometric means of serum neutralizing titers were observed for SARS-CoV-2
spike-specific binding IgG concentrations. All groups showed an increase vs. baseline at Day 29 for both
antigens, and a gradual decrease up to Day 181, which remained above baseline (Figures 4C and 4D). The
CV0701 groups showed a dose-dependent response at all post-vaccination timepoints, and the CV0601
group had numerically higher SARS-CoV-2 spike-specific binding IgG concentrations compared to the
CV0701-High group for the Omicron BA.4–5 antigen and similar concentrations as the CV0701-High
group for the ancestral D614G antigen (Figures 4C and 4D).


Cell-mediated immunity

The geometric mean frequency (GMF) of ancestral D614G and Omicron BA.4-5-specific polypositive CD4
+ T cells increased from pre-dose (Day 1) to Day 8 in all study groups (Figure 5(A)). When looking at the
individual fold-change, most participants had a 1- to 2-fold increase, with only a few showing ≥2-fold
increase. CD4+ T cells expressing at least IFN-γ (Th1 helper profile) increased in all study groups, while
CD4+ T cells expressing at least IL-13 (Th2 helper profile) or at least IL-17 (Th17 helper profile) did not
increase in any of the groups (Supplementary Table S3).
  An increased GMF of ancestral D614G and Omicron BA.4-5-specific polypositive CD8+ T cells was
observed from Day 1 to Day 8 for the two highest doses of CV0701, as well as in the CV0601 and the
comparator groups (Figure 5(B), Supplementary Table S3). Similar to CD4+ polypositive T cells, individual
participants showed a 1- to 2-fold increase with only a few showing an ≥2-fold increase (Supplementary
Table S3). The GMF of the CD8+ T cells co-expressing HLA-DR+ and CD38+ increased from pre-dose
(Day 1) to Day 8 in all study groups (Supplementary Table S3).


Discussion

In the current phase 2 study, we investigated the reactogenicity, safety and immunogenicity of two
investigational mRNA COVID-19 vaccines, one bivalent at three dose levels and one monovalent at one
dose level, and compared the results to a licensed, bivalent mRNA COVID-19 vaccine. Similar to licensed
COVID-19 vaccines, for which the target antigens are updated according to the Food and Drug
Administration and the World Health Organization recommendations, our expectation is that the present
investigational vaccine will be updated accordingly.

  The demography of the study population was balanced between the study groups, and  all
participants were generally healthy without signs of current infection. As expected in a population-
level  setting, a similar number of participants reported a prior SARS-CoV-2 infection or were
positive for anti-N antibody pre-vaccination. The number of prior vaccinations was similar across
groups.
  Our results show that most solicited events within seven days post-vaccination were mild or moderate in
intensity and resolved within a few days. No imbalance was observed for overall unsolicited AEs reported
across study groups within 28 d post-vaccination. Overall MAAEs reported up to study end were balanced
between groups. MAAEs related to the study vaccination were limited (0% to 1.2%). None of the SAEs nor
AESIs reported up to study end were assessed as related to study vaccination, and no SAEs with fatal
outcome were reported.
  The safety profile of both investigational mRNA vaccines was similar to the licensed, bivalent mRNA
comparator vaccine. While an increased risk for myocarditis or pericarditis with mRNA COVID-19
vaccines has been reported,19 we did not observe such events in the current study. However, this may be
due to the limited sample size.
  The immunogenicity results showed a dose-dependent increase in neutralizing titers against both pseu­
doviruses bearing the Omicron BA.4–5 and the ancestral D614G spike proteins for the bivalent CV0701
mRNA vaccine at Day 29 post-vaccination. Neutralizing titers declined, but persisted up to Day 181 post-
vaccination, similar to the comparator vaccine. The monovalent CV0601 mRNA vaccine showed a similar
immune response to the highest dose of the CV0701 mRNA vaccine. When comparing to the comparator
vaccine, all but the lowest dose of the CV0701 mRNA vaccine showed numerically higher neutralizing titers at
all timepoints. While baseline neutralizing titers were lower in the comparator group than in the investiga­
tional groups, the GMT ratios were baseline-adjusted to correct for this observation. Neutralizing titers can be
interpreted as supportive immunological markers rather than definitive predictors of clinical protection.
  For the Omicron BA.4–5 variant, all investigational groups except the CV0701-Low group had a similar
proportion of seroresponders at Day 29, which was similar to the comparator group. For the ancestral
D614G variant, the proportion of seroresponders was lower when compared to the Omicron BA.4–5
variant. At Day 91 and Day 181, neutralizing titers remained above baseline titers, but were lower compared
to Day 29, which is consistent with other mRNA vaccines.20,21
  The Omicron BA.4–5 antigen responses were similar in the CV0601 group and the CV0701 groups,
indicating that the addition of the ancestral D614G component to the bivalent formulation did not impair
the antibody responses to the Omicron BA.4–5 variant. Interestingly, we observed high neutralizing titers to
the ancestral D614G variant in participants who received the CV0601 mRNA vaccine, which encodes the
Omicron BA.4–5 antigen. This observation suggests that the updated, variant-specific vaccine (e.g., for
Omicron BA.4–5) does not diminish a participant’s preexisting immune responses to the ancestral D614G
variant, whether those responses were acquired through prior infection or vaccination.
   Post-vaccination, we observed an increase in anti-spike-specific polypositive CD4+ T cells targeting both
ancestral D614G and Omicron BA.4-5 variants in all groups. This finding is consistent with a previous study
in a similar primed boost setting.22 Furthermore, the CD4+ T-cell response was predominantly skewed
toward a Th1 helper profile response. For polypositive CD8+ T cells, the GMF changes were comparable
between the CV0701-Med and -High groups, the CV0601 group, and the comparator group. While at the
individual level some participants showed a higher CD8+ T-cell response, the overlapping CIs pre- and
post-vaccination indicate no significant difference between groups. A consistent in vivo activation of CD8+
T cells upon vaccination was noted, with comparable increases between the CV0701-Med and -High groups
and the comparator group.
  The key strengths of our study are the randomized, active-controlled, i.e., using a licensed comparator,
observer-blind design and contemporaneous enrollment. As is the case for other early phase vaccine studies
which are not able to show rare events due to limitations in sample size, this study was not powered to
identify rare events. Moreover, the absence of formal hypothesis testing limits the ability to draw definitive
comparative or inferential conclusions. The participants’ demographics are reflective of the Australian
population, which might limit the generalizability of our results. Additional studies in larger and more
diverse populations will be required to confirm generalizability of these findings and strengthen the
precision of the safety and immunogenicity estimates. We also hypothesize that the investigational vaccine

may offer a dose-sparing advantage over the comparator vaccine in terms of reactogenicity, manufacturing
and efficiency; however, larger studies are required to confirm this hypothesis.
   In conclusion, both bivalent CV0701 and monovalent CV0601 mRNA vaccine candidates had an
acceptable safety profile and induced a robust immune response at Day 29 post-vaccination. This immune
response declined, but persisted up to Day 181. These results provide critical insights for continued
COVID-19 mRNA vaccine development efforts aimed at addressing the continuous medical need.

message.content: This phase 2, randomized, active-controlled, observer-blind study evaluated the safety, reactogenicity, and immunogenicity of two investigational mRNA vaccines against SARS-CoV-2, compared to a licensed bivalent mRNA vaccine. The study included 425 healthy adults aged ≥18 years who had completed a primary vaccination series with or without a booster at least three months prior. Participants were randomized to receive either a bivalent mRNA vaccine (CV0701) encoding ancestral D614G and Omicron BA.4–5 spike proteins at three dose levels, a monovalent mRNA vaccine (CV0601) encoding Omicron BA.4–5 spike protein, or a licensed comparator vaccine. The primary endpoints were reactogenicity, safety, and immunogenicity, with secondary and tertiary endpoints focusing on humoral and cell-mediated immune responses. Most solicited events were mild to moderate, and no vaccine-related serious adverse events or cases of myocarditis/pericarditis were reported. For the CV0701 vaccine, neutralizing titers against both ancestral D614G and Omicron BA.4–5 increased dose-dependently at Day 29 and remained above baseline at Day 181. The CV0601 vaccine showed similar immune responses. CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell responses were observed in all groups, with the lowest dose of CV0701 showing a lesser response. The investigational vaccines demonstrated an acceptable safety profile and robust immunogenicity, comparable to the licensed comparator vaccine. The study limitations include the small sample size and lack of formal hypothesis testing, which may limit the ability to detect rare events or draw definitive comparative conclusions. These findings support the potential of these vaccines in addressing the evolving SARS-CoV-2 variants.

message.content: A phase 2 study evaluated the safety and immunogenicity of two investigational mRNA vaccines against SARS-CoV-2, compared to a licensed bivalent vaccine. Both investigational vaccines showed dose-dependent increases in neutralizing antibodies and T-cell responses, with an acceptable safety profile. However, the small sample size and lack of formal hypothesis testing limit the ability to draw definitive conclusions about their comparative efficacy.
